source.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. The Methods text has a missing sequence-identity threshold after “must be”.
record.tranche_reason: Compares downstream task accuracy across differently sized language models, bearing on V6, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy or reproduce the original loss-scaling method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and calls its biological-task results a qualitative scaling law. It reports downstream accuracy, not cross-entropy loss, token or compute scaling, or fitted predictive curves. The results below bear only on V6. Interpretability results and scores on tasks without a scale comparison are not additional evidence for the power-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares a biological downstream task across model tiers (GPT-2 0.1B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen-3/Gemini-3) and calls the result a 'qualitative scaling law'. That bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. It is not T2: no loss, no controlled size sweep and no fitted curve. Model family, tuning, prompting and readout (logits vs chat) all change between tiers.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim cross-modal transfer from English paraphrase tuning to biology and a 'qualitative scaling law' across GPT-2, Llama 8B and Qwen-3. However, they present the 8B result (75%) as scaling progress even though their own fine-tuned GPT-2 scored higher (84%). They report no loss or fitted scaling relation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates accuracy on biological tasks across heterogeneous models and training or prompting setups; it does not conduct the original loss-versus-parameters, tokens, or compute experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different outcomes with base versus instruction-fine-tuned Llama 3.1, English-only versus biologically exposed GPT-2, and different biological tasks and prompting setups.
record.problems: The reported accuracy for fine-tuned GPT-2 is inconsistent (80% in the Fig. 1 caption versus a peak of 84.0% in the results and Fig. 2). The model comparisons use differing tuning and prompting procedures and do not form a controlled size sweep. Most scores have no reported error bars or confidence intervals; the Methods section omits the remote-homology sequence-identity threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying downstream accuracy results were left out. Interpretability measures, cited work, and results that do not compare downstream performance across models were not included.

untested.parts: Predictability: no curve or fit against parameters or loss, no controlled within-family size sweep, no test against pretraining loss.
No power-law fits on biological data.

missing.what: Specialized PLMs (ESM-2/ProtT5): ~100% standard vs ~50% remote homology. This is not a scale comparison but is relevant context for the general-LM tiers.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence on V6 is weak and heavily confounded: different model families, fine-tuning vs zero-shot prompting, and logits vs chat readout across tiers. The Qwen-3 '>1000B' size is unverified. The Fig. 1 GPT-2 accuracy (80%) conflicts with the text (84-85%). Error bars are absent, and the remote-homology identity threshold is missing from Methods.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or power-law relation to parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No power-law fit on small runs or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is measured.
No comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count is reported.
Biological input tasks are evaluated, but the study does not test whether a power-law loss form carries over to other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports accuracy on biological tasks across several models and sizes, but does not fit a predictive relation, test performance against pretraining loss, or use a controlled size sweep.
The study does not vary loss-fitting choices or compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits.

relationships.condition: Largest vs smallest tier, standard protein and DNA homology (heterogeneous models, tuning and prompts)
relationships.reason: Qwen-3 reaches ~100% vs fine-tuned GPT-2 at 84% (protein) and 78% (DNA). The direction matches V6 but is confounded (r2, r9, r13, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Qwen-3 reached approximately 100% versus fine-tuned GPT-2 at 84% for protein and 78% for DNA homology, with model, tuning and prompt differences confounding the comparison.

relationships.condition: Intermediate 8B tier and base models on protein homology; Central Dogma task
relationships.reason: Gains are non-monotonic: Llama 8B FT is at 75%, below GPT-2 0.1B at 84%, and Llama base at ~50% is no better than raw GPT-2. On Central Dogma, bio data exposure rather than scale accounts for most of the gain (r2, r3, r7, r8, r1, r17).
relationships.display_finding: On protein homology, fine-tuned Llama 8B scored 75% versus GPT-2 0.1B's 84% and base Llama remained near 50% like raw GPT-2, while biological data exposure explained most Central Dogma gains.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reported biological downstream-task results across the paper
reader_labels.reason: The study gives task accuracies across models, but does not establish predictable improvement with scale: tuning, prompts, tasks, and evaluation procedures vary, and no predictive curve is fitted (r1-r3, r7-r18).
